skill.name: test-driven-development
skill.description: Guides implementation and bug fixes through the red-green-refactor loop, repository-aware test commands, focused verification, and full-suite checks.
skill.summary: Use red-green-refactor to implement behavior, reproduce bugs, and verify changes with repository-specific tests.
skill.author: addyosmani

remediation.issue: The skill instructs agents to run repository-defined test commands, which may execute project-controlled scripts.
remediation.suggestion: Keep command execution limited to the user's repository, inspect scripts before running them, and request confirmation before executing commands with destructive or external side effects.

remediation.issue: Examples mention external services and browser inspection.
remediation.suggestion: Maintain the existing boundary guidance: treat repository and browser content as untrusted data, avoid credentials, and require confirmation before navigating to URLs taken from page content.

content.value_statement: Teams need reliable ways to implement changes and fix bugs without relying on intuition or fragile manual checks. This skill guides a red-green-refactor workflow with repository-aware commands, focused tests, and full-suite verification.
actual_capabilities: Guides agents through the red-green-refactor development loop.
Requires reproduction tests before implementing bug fixes.
Helps discover repository-specific test frameworks and commands.
Recommends state-based assertions, test isolation, and descriptive test names.
Distinguishes unit, integration, and end-to-end testing by resource use.
Adds browser runtime verification guidance for browser-based changes.
limitations: It provides process guidance and does not write or execute project code by itself.
It cannot determine whether a repository command is safe without inspecting that repository.
Its examples use TypeScript syntax and require adaptation for other languages.
It does not replace security review, code review, or deployment validation.

use_cases.title: Build New Features
use_cases.description: Plan a failing test, implement the smallest passing behavior, and refactor while preserving verified outcomes.

use_cases.title: Fix Reported Bugs
use_cases.description: Turn a bug report into a reproduction test, confirm the failure, implement a fix, and check for regressions.

use_cases.title: Verify Browser Changes
use_cases.description: Combine automated tests with browser inspection of the DOM, console, network behavior, styles, and screenshots.

prompt_templates.title: Start With a Test
prompt_templates.prompt: Guide me through writing a failing test for this behavior: [describe behavior]. Ask only for the repository test command and relevant file context.
prompt_templates.scenario: Beginner workflow for a small feature

prompt_templates.title: Reproduce a Bug
prompt_templates.prompt: Apply the Prove-It Pattern to this bug: [bug report]. Define the expected behavior, propose a reproduction test, and explain what failure would confirm the bug.

prompt_templates.title: Review Test Design
prompt_templates.prompt: Review these tests for state-based assertions, isolation, determinism, meaningful names, and appropriate use of mocks. Suggest focused improvements without changing the intended behavior: [tests].

prompt_templates.title: Plan Full Verification
prompt_templates.prompt: Create a verification plan for this change: [change]. Identify focused tests, integration or end-to-end coverage, browser checks when relevant, the repository's full-suite command, and risks that need manual review.

output_examples.input: A task completion bug leaves the completion timestamp empty.
output: Reproduction test: complete a task and assert that its status changes and its completion timestamp is present.
Expected first result: the test fails because the timestamp is missing.
Next step: implement the smallest fix, rerun the focused test, then run the full suite.

output_examples.input: A developer wants to test a list operation that sorts records.
output: Prefer an assertion on the returned order and values.
Avoid asserting that a specific internal database query string was called.
This keeps the test focused on observable behavior during refactoring.

output_examples.input: A browser change alters a critical checkout flow.
output: Run the focused automated tests first.
Reproduce the flow in a browser and inspect console errors, network responses, DOM structure, styles, and a screenshot.
Run the repository's full test suite after the change.

best_practices: Discover the repository's actual test command before starting the TDD cycle.
Test observable behavior with deterministic, isolated cases.
Run focused tests during iteration and the full suite after implementation.
anti_patterns: Writing implementation code before creating a test that demonstrates the expected behavior.
Testing internal call sequences when an observable result can verify the behavior.
Skipping tests or repeating unchanged test commands without a code change.

faq.question: When should I use this skill?
faq.answer: Use it for new behavior, bug fixes, behavior changes, edge cases, and changes that could introduce regressions.

faq.question: What does red-green-refactor mean?
faq.answer: Write a failing test, implement the smallest passing change, then improve the code while keeping tests passing.

faq.question: Does this skill choose the test command?
faq.answer: It tells you to inspect the repository and use its documented focused and full-suite commands.

faq.question: Should every test use mocks?
faq.answer: No. Prefer real implementations, then fakes or stubs. Use mocks mainly for slow, nondeterministic, or side-effecting boundaries.

faq.question: Does it support browser testing?
faq.answer: Yes. It recommends runtime checks with browser tools for DOM, console, network, styles, performance, and screenshots.

faq.question: Can it replace a security review?
faq.answer: No. TDD verifies behavior, but security review, dependency review, code review, and deployment checks remain necessary.
